API reference¶

Data loading¶

Load the NASA/UCI Airfoil Self-Noise dataset.

The dataset contains 1503 aerodynamic/acoustic measurements of NACA 0012 airfoils taken in a wind tunnel. Five input features describe the test conditions and one target, the scaled sound pressure level, describes the measured noise.

The Excel file is expected at data/airfoil_self_noise.xlsx. It is not committed to the repository and must be kept locally, as noted in the project README.

Example

>>> from functions.data_loader import load_airfoil_data
>>> df = load_airfoil_data()
>>> df.columns.tolist()[-1]
'spl_db'
functions.data_loader.DATA_PATH = WindowsPath('C:/Users/vasbr/OneDrive/Desktop/uni mech eng/2026s2/mma3001 numerical methods and machine learning/mma3001project/nummethodproject/data/airfoil_self_noise.xlsx')¶

Physics features¶

Physics-derived features for the airfoil self-noise dataset.

The raw inputs are dimensional, but airfoil noise is governed largely by dimensionless groups. This module adds three engineered features computed row-wise from the raw columns, so they are recomputed on every load rather than stored in the Excel file.

Example

>>> from functions.data_loader import load_airfoil_data
>>> from functions.physics_features import add_physics_features
>>> df = add_physics_features(load_airfoil_data())
>>> df[["log_frequency", "strouhal", "reynolds"]].shape[1]
3
functions.physics_features.KINEMATIC_VISCOSITY_M2PS = 1.5e-05¶

Kinematic viscosity of air at roughly 20 °C (m^2/s), used for the Reynolds number. The wind-tunnel temperature is not recorded in the dataset, so a standard room-temperature value is assumed.

functions.physics_features.PHYSICS_FEATURES = ['log_frequency', 'strouhal', 'reynolds']¶

Names of the columns added by add_physics_features().

functions.physics_features.add_physics_features(df: pandas.DataFrame) → pandas.DataFrame[source]¶

Return a copy of the dataset with physics-derived feature columns.

Adds:

  • log_frequency: log10(frequency_hz). Frequencies span about two decades, and acoustic spectra are naturally read on a log axis.

  • strouhal: frequency_hz * disp_thickness_m / velocity_mps. Uses the suction-side displacement thickness as the length scale, the scaling used for turbulent boundary-layer trailing-edge noise in the Brooks-Pope-Marcolini (BPM) model.

  • reynolds: velocity_mps * chord_length_m / nu, the chord-based Reynolds number with nu = KINEMATIC_VISCOSITY_M2PS.

Each feature depends only on its own row, so adding them before the train/validation/test split does not leak information between sets.

Parameters:

df – Dataset as returned by functions.data_loader.load_airfoil_data().

Returns:

A new DataFrame with the original columns plus the columns listed in PHYSICS_FEATURES. The input DataFrame is not modified.

Data split¶

Grouped, chord-stratified test hold-out and 5-fold cross-validation split.

Each wind-tunnel setup (a unique chord length, free-stream velocity and angle of attack) contributes one noise spectrum of 8-19 rows. Rows from the same spectrum are strongly correlated, so whole setups are assigned to a split: a setup’s rows are never divided between training and validation/test.

The split is stratified on chord length because chord is the only variable tested at the same values throughout the dataset; the angles tested differ for every chord and some velocity/angle combinations were never measured.

Splitting happens on a table with one row per setup, so ordinary stratified splitters give a grouped split automatically. The result is mapped back onto the measurement rows as two columns:

  • setup_id: integer id of the setup, numbered in order of (chord, velocity, angle).

  • fold: 0 to N_FOLDS - 1 for cross-validation rows, or TEST_FOLD for rows in the held-out test set.

Example

>>> from functions.data_loader import load_airfoil_data
>>> from functions.make_folds import assign_folds, CV_SEEDS, TEST_FOLD
>>> raw = load_airfoil_data()
>>> for seed in CV_SEEDS:
...     df = assign_folds(raw, cv_seed=seed)
...     test = df[df["fold"] == TEST_FOLD]  # same setups for every seed
...     cv = df[df["fold"] != TEST_FOLD]
functions.make_folds.SETUP_KEYS = ['chord_length_m', 'velocity_mps', 'attack_angle_deg']¶

Columns that together identify one wind-tunnel setup.

functions.make_folds.STRATIFY_ON = 'chord_length_m'¶

Column the split is stratified on.

functions.make_folds.N_FOLDS = 5¶

Number of cross-validation folds.

functions.make_folds.TEST_FRACTION = 0.15¶

Fraction of setups held out as the untouched test set.

functions.make_folds.TEST_FOLD = -1¶

fold value given to rows in the held-out test set.

functions.make_folds.TEST_SEED = 41¶

Seed for the test hold-out, distinct from every CV seed. Kept fixed across CV repeats so the test set stays the same setups and is never used for tuning in any repeat.

functions.make_folds.CV_SEEDS = [42, 43, 44]¶

Seeds for repeated cross-validation. Each seed reshuffles the 5 folds within the same non-test setups; averaging scores over all repeats shows how much results depend on the particular split.

functions.make_folds.assign_folds(df: pandas.DataFrame, n_folds: int = 5, test_fraction: float = 0.15, cv_seed: int = 42, test_seed: int = 41) → pandas.DataFrame[source]¶

Return a copy of the dataset with setup_id and fold columns.

First holds out test_fraction of the setups as a test set, then splits the remaining setups into n_folds cross-validation folds. Both steps are stratified on chord length and work on whole setups. For repeated CV, call once per seed in CV_SEEDS; the test set depends only on test_seed and so is identical across repeats.

Parameters:

  • df – Dataset as returned by functions.data_loader.load_airfoil_data() (physics feature columns, if present, are carried through unchanged).

  • n_folds – Number of cross-validation folds.

  • test_fraction – Fraction of setups held out as the test set.

  • cv_seed – Random seed for shuffling setups into CV folds.

  • test_seed – Random seed for choosing the test hold-out.

Returns:

A new DataFrame with the original columns plus setup_id and fold. The input DataFrame is not modified.

Feature sets¶

Named input feature sets, so models can be compared on different inputs.

Each feature set is a list of column names. Any model in functions.models can be trained on any feature set, so swapping inputs is a matter of changing one name.

  • A: the five raw wind-tunnel inputs.

  • B: A plus the physics-derived features log_frequency, strouhal and reynolds. These columns only exist after functions.physics_features.add_physics_features() has been applied.

Example

>>> from functions.feature_sets import get_feature_columns
>>> get_feature_columns("B")[-3:]
['log_frequency', 'strouhal', 'reynolds']
functions.feature_sets.FEATURE_SETS = {'A': ['frequency_hz', 'attack_angle_deg', 'chord_length_m', 'velocity_mps', 'disp_thickness_m'], 'B': ['frequency_hz', 'attack_angle_deg', 'chord_length_m', 'velocity_mps', 'disp_thickness_m', 'log_frequency', 'strouhal', 'reynolds']}¶

Feature set name -> input columns. Add a new entry here to make another set available to every model and to src/run_cv.py.

Raises:

Models¶

Model registry: every model is built as the same scikit-learn pipeline.

Each model returned by build_model() has the structure:

TransformedTargetRegressor(
    regressor=Pipeline([("scaler", StandardScaler()),   # if scale_inputs
                        ("regressor", <estimator>)]),
    transformer=StandardScaler(),                       # scales spl_db
)

Because the scalers sit inside the estimator, calling fit on the training rows fits them on those rows only; validation and test rows are transformed with the training mean and standard deviation and never influence them.

Scaling the target to zero mean and unit variance matters for SVR (its epsilon tube and C are in target units) and for neural networks (output scale and loss magnitude). For the linear baseline neither scaling step changes the predictions, but it is applied anyway so every model runs through the same pipeline and the linear coefficients are comparable in size.

Two models are registered:

  • "linear": ordinary least squares, the baseline.

  • "mlp": a multi-layer perceptron (MLPRegressor) with early stopping. The layer sizes and alpha set here are only defaults; the values actually reported come from nested cross-validation in functions.tuning.

Tree-based models and SVR are planned; each is added as one ModelSpec entry in MODELS (trees do not need input scaling, so they would use scale_inputs=False).

Example

>>> from functions.models import build_model
>>> model = build_model("linear")
>>> model.fit(X_train, y_train).predict(X_val)
functions.models.MLP_DEFAULTS = {'alpha': 0.001, 'early_stopping': True, 'hidden_layer_sizes': (64, 64), 'max_iter': 2000, 'n_iter_no_change': 20, 'random_state': 0, 'tol': 0.0001, 'validation_fraction': 0.1}¶

Default MLP settings. Hidden layer sizes and alpha are tuned by functions.tuning; the rest are fixed for every fit.

class functions.models.ModelSpec(make: Callable[[], RegressorMixin], scale_inputs: bool = True)[source]¶

How to build one registered model.

Variables:

  • make (collections.abc.Callable[[], sklearn.base.RegressorMixin]) – Zero-argument callable returning a new, unfitted estimator. A fresh estimator is needed for every fold so no fitted state is shared between folds.

  • scale_inputs (bool) – Whether to standardise the inputs before the estimator. Needed for distance- and gradient-based models (SVR, MLP), unnecessary for trees.

make: Callable[[], RegressorMixin]¶
scale_inputs: bool = True¶
functions.models.MODELS = {'linear': ModelSpec(make=<class 'sklearn.linear_model._base.LinearRegression'>, scale_inputs=True), 'mlp': ModelSpec(make=<function _make_mlp>, scale_inputs=True)}¶

Model name -> ModelSpec. Add planned models (tree-based, SVR) here; anything with randomness must be given a fixed random_state so results are reproducible.

functions.models.build_model(name: str) → TransformedTargetRegressor[source]¶

Build a new, unfitted model wrapped in the standard scaling pipeline.

Parameters:

name – Key of MODELS, e.g. "linear".

Returns:

A TransformedTargetRegressor whose inner regressor is a Pipeline of an optional input StandardScaler and the estimator. The target is standardised by a second StandardScaler and predictions are converted back to dB automatically.

Raises:

KeyError – If name is not a registered model.

functions.models.coefficient_effects(model: TransformedTargetRegressor, feature_names: list[str]) → pd.Series | None[source]¶

Return a fitted linear model’s coefficients as dB per standard deviation.

Inside the pipeline both inputs and target are standardised, so each fitted coefficient is the change in SPL, in target standard deviations, for a one-standard-deviation change in that input with all other inputs held fixed. Multiplying by the target’s standard deviation turns this into dB per input standard deviation, which can be compared directly across features with very different units (Hz, m, m/s, Reynolds number).

Correlated inputs (e.g. frequency_hz and log_frequency in set B) share their effect between them, so individual coefficients can be large, of opposite sign and unstable between folds even when predictions are good. Look at the spread over folds before interpreting one.

Parameters:

  • model – A model from build_model() that has been fitted.

  • feature_names – Input columns in the order the model was fitted on.

Returns:

A Series indexed by feature name, in dB per input standard deviation, or None if the model has no linear coefficients or does not scale its inputs (raw-unit coefficients are not comparable across features).

Cross-validation and metrics¶

Repeated cross-validation, metrics and error breakdowns for any model.

cross_validate() trains a model from functions.models on a feature set from functions.feature_sets using the grouped folds from functions.make_folds, repeated for every seed in CV_SEEDS. It returns:

  • per-fold scores (RMSE, MAE, R², fit and predict time), and

  • out-of-fold (OOF) predictions: every cross-validation row predicted once per seed by the model that did not see it during training.

Rows in the held-out test set are dropped before anything is fitted, so this module never trains on, tunes on or scores the test set.

RMSE is the main metric. oof_rmse_breakdown() splits the OOF RMSE by chord length, free-stream velocity, angle-of-attack band and frequency band to show where a model’s errors come from. For linear models, coefficient_summary() reports each input’s effect in dB per standard deviation and how stable it is across folds.

Example

>>> from functions.data_loader import load_airfoil_data
>>> from functions.physics_features import add_physics_features
>>> from functions.evaluate import cross_validate, summarise, oof_rmse_breakdown
>>> data = add_physics_features(load_airfoil_data())
>>> result = cross_validate(data, "linear", "A")
>>> summarise(result)            
>>> oof_rmse_breakdown(result)

functions.evaluate.cross_validate(data: pandas.DataFrame, model_name: str, feature_set: str, cv_seeds: list[int] = [42, 43, 44]) → CVResult[source]¶

Run repeated grouped k-fold cross-validation for one model/feature set.

For each seed, functions.make_folds.assign_folds() assigns folds, the test hold-out is dropped, and for each fold a fresh model is fitted on the other folds and predicts the held-out fold. Fit and predict are timed separately with time.perf_counter().

Parameters:

  • data – Dataset from functions.data_loader.load_airfoil_data(). It must already contain any columns the feature set needs (call functions.physics_features.add_physics_features() for set B).

  • model_name – Key of functions.models.MODELS.

  • feature_set – Key of functions.feature_sets.FEATURE_SETS.

  • cv_seeds – Seeds for repeated CV. Defaults to functions.make_folds.CV_SEEDS and should not be changed when comparing models.

Returns:

A CVResult with per-fold scores, OOF predictions and, for linear models, per-fold coefficients.

Raises:

KeyError – If the model or feature set name is unknown, or data is missing a column the feature set needs.

functions.evaluate.summarise(result: CVResult) → dict[str, float][source]¶

Summarise a CV run as one row of headline numbers.

Each metric is the mean and sample standard deviation of the per-fold validation scores over all folds of all seeds (15 for 5 folds x 3 seeds). Each fold scores a model on a batch of setups it never saw, so the standard deviation answers “how much does the score change from one batch of unseen setups to the next?”. This is wider than the spread of seed-level averages, which would only show how much the random fold shuffle matters. Timings are also averaged over all folds.

The mean of per-fold RMSEs is slightly different from the RMSE of all pooled OOF predictions, because the square root is taken per fold.

Parameters:

result – Output of cross_validate().

Returns:

A dict with model, feature_set, n_folds (number of fold scores averaged), rmse, rmse_std, mae, mae_std, r2, r2_std, fit_time_s and predict_time_s (mean seconds per fold).

functions.evaluate.oof_rmse_breakdown(result: CVResult) → pandas.DataFrame[source]¶

Break the OOF RMSE down by chord, velocity, angle band and frequency band.

For each breakdown column and each group within it, RMSE is computed on that group’s OOF predictions separately for every seed, then averaged over seeds.

Parameters:

result – Output of cross_validate().

Returns:

A DataFrame with columns breakdown (which column was grouped on), group (the value or band label), n (rows per seed), rmse (mean over seeds, dB) and rmse_std (std over seeds).

functions.evaluate.coefficient_summary(result: CVResult) → pandas.DataFrame[source]¶

Summarise a linear model’s per-fold coefficients.

Every (seed, fold) fit gives one coefficient per feature; this reports their mean and spread. A coefficient whose sign flips between folds, or whose std is comparable to its mean, is not reliably estimated and should not be given a physical interpretation.

Parameters:

result – Output of cross_validate().

Returns:

A DataFrame indexed by feature (in feature-set order) with columns effect_db_per_sd (mean over fits), std, min, max and sign_agreement (fraction of fits whose sign matches the mean’s). Empty if the model has no linear coefficients.

functions.evaluate.SETUP_COLUMNS = ['setup_id', 'chord_length_m', 'velocity_mps', 'attack_angle_deg']¶

Columns describing one wind-tunnel setup in per_setup_rmse().

functions.evaluate.per_setup_rmse(result: CVResult, data: pandas.DataFrame) → pandas.DataFrame[source]¶

Out-of-fold error for every wind-tunnel setup (one noise spectrum each).

In each CV repeat a setup sits in exactly one validation fold, so it is predicted once per seed by a model that never saw it. The setup’s RMSE is computed separately for each seed and then averaged over seeds. The bias (mean of measured minus predicted) shows whether the model sits mostly above or below the measured spectrum.

Parameters:

  • result – Output of cross_validate() (or the tuned-MLP equivalent from functions.tuning).

  • data – The dataset the result was computed on.

Returns:

One row per setup, worst first, with columns setup_id, chord_length_m, velocity_mps, attack_angle_deg, n_rows (measurements in the spectrum), rmse (dB, mean over seeds), rmse_sd_seeds and bias (dB; positive means the model under-predicts).

Entry point that cross-validates models on feature sets and reports results.

Every combination of the requested models and feature sets is evaluated with repeated grouped 5-fold CV (functions.evaluate.cross_validate()). The test hold-out is never used. Defaults run the linear baseline on sets A and B:

python src/run_cv.py
python src/run_cv.py --models linear --feature-sets A

Results are printed and written as CSV files to results/:

  • cv_summary.csv: one row per model/feature set (validation RMSE, MAE, R² as mean and std over all 15 folds, 5 folds x 3 seeds; mean fit and predict time per fold).

  • cv_fold_scores.csv: scores and timings for every seed and fold.

  • cv_rmse_breakdown.csv: OOF RMSE by chord, velocity, angle band and frequency band.

  • cv_coefficients.csv: for linear models, each input’s effect in dB per standard deviation (mean and spread over all folds and seeds).

Rounded copies of the summary, breakdown and coefficient tables, and the results figures (functions.plot_results), are also written to doc/generated/ for the HTML results page; rebuild the docs afterwards to publish them.

Results figures¶

Figures of cross-validation results for the HTML results page.

Every function takes one or more functions.evaluate.CVResult objects and returns a matplotlib figure; save_result_figures() draws them all and writes PNGs. Each result keeps the same colour in every figure (first result blue, second orange, …), so a model/feature set is recognisable across the page. Measured data are drawn in neutral ink, never a series colour.

Figures that show individual predictions use one CV seed (functions.make_folds.CV_SEEDS [0] by default) so that every row appears exactly once.

Example

>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from functions.evaluate import cross_validate
>>> from functions.plot_results import save_result_figures
>>> results = [cross_validate(data, "linear", fs) for fs in ("A", "B")]
>>> save_result_figures(data, results, Path("doc/generated"))

MLP tuning (nested cross-validation)¶

Nested cross-validation to tune and fairly score the MLP.

Why nested CV?

If the same folds were used both to pick the best hyperparameters and to report the score, the score would be optimistic: the chosen setting is partly the one that got lucky on those folds. Nested CV keeps the two jobs apart. An inner CV, run on the outer training rows only, picks the hyperparameters; the outer validation fold, which the inner CV never sees, then scores the chosen model. The outer scores are therefore honest estimates for unseen setups.

Procedure (nested_cv()), for each seed in CV_SEEDS and each outer fold:

  1. Drop the test hold-out (it is never used for training, tuning, early stopping or scoring here). Outer validation = rows of this fold; outer training = the other cross-validation rows.

  2. On the outer training rows only, GridSearchCV tries every setting in PARAM_GRID with an inner grouped 5-fold split (inner_splitter()). setup_id is passed as groups, so no setup is ever split between inner training and inner validation.

  3. The best setting is refitted on all outer training rows and scored on the outer validation fold (RMSE, MAE, R² in dB).

Known limitations (quotable in the report):

  • Early stopping uses random rows, not whole setups. MLPRegressor’s built-in early stopping holds back a random 10% of the rows it is given to decide when to stop. Rows from one setup are strongly correlated, so the held-back rows usually have near-identical neighbours from the same setup in the training part. The internal stopping check is therefore mildly optimistic, and training may stop a little later than ideal. This does not leak into the reported scores: the inner and outer validation folds are grouped by setup, and the early-stopping rows are taken only from the data being fitted, never from the fold being scored. MLPRegressor was deliberately not rewritten to fix this.

  • Inner folds are grouped but not stratified on chord. GroupKFold keeps setups together but does not balance chord lengths across inner folds (the outer folds are chord-stratified by functions.make_folds.assign_folds()).

  • Convergence. Fits that stop at max_iter rather than by early stopping are counted (_hit_max_iter()), not hidden. Warnings raised in parallel worker processes cannot be caught in the main process, so the count is collected as an extra “score” instead.

Example

>>> from functions.tuning import nested_cv
>>> result = nested_cv(data, "A", seeds=[42])   
>>> result.outer_scores[["seed", "fold", "rmse"]]

functions.tuning.refit_outer_predictions(data: pandas.DataFrame, outer_scores: pandas.DataFrame, feature_set: str, extra_params: dict | None = None, atol: float = 1e-06) → CVResult[source]¶

Rebuild the tuned MLP’s out-of-fold predictions from saved results.

tuning_outer_scores.csv records which setting won each outer fold but not the row-by-row predictions. Because the MLP has a fixed random_state and is trained on exactly the same rows, refitting the winning setting reproduces each fold’s model, and so its predictions, exactly. This takes seconds instead of re-running the whole nested CV. Each refitted fold’s RMSE is checked against the saved value as proof.

Parameters:

  • data – Dataset with every column the feature set needs.

  • outer_scores – The saved TuningResult.outer_scores table (e.g. read from results/tuning_outer_scores.csv).

  • feature_set – Which feature set’s rows to rebuild.

  • extra_params – Further fixed model parameters that were in the search grid (none for the standard grid; used by the tests).

  • atol – Largest allowed difference between refitted and saved RMSE.

Returns:

A CVResult (model "mlp (tuned)") with per-fold scores and OOF predictions.

Raises:

ValueError – If no rows match feature_set, or a refitted fold’s RMSE differs from the saved one (the saved results then came from different code or data).

Figures for the nested-CV tuning of the MLP.

  • plot_inner_grid_heatmap(): mean inner-CV RMSE for every setting in the grid, showing which layer sizes and alphas work and whether the best one sits at the edge of the grid.

  • plot_loss_curves(): training loss and internal validation score per epoch for the chosen model in a few outer folds, showing where early stopping ended training.

Predicted-vs-measured and RMSE-breakdown comparisons reuse functions.plot_results directly. save_png_pdf() writes every figure as PNG (for the HTML docs) and PDF (vector, for the report). The visual style matches functions.plot_results.

functions.plot_tuning.plot_loss_curves(result: TuningResult, keys: list[tuple[int, int]]) → matplotlib.figure.Figure[source]¶

Training loss and early-stopping score per epoch for chosen models.

Top row: training loss (half the mean squared error on the standardised target, plus the L2 penalty). Bottom row: R² on the random 10% of rows that MLPRegressor holds back for early stopping. The dashed line marks the epoch with the highest validation score. Training stops once the score has failed to beat its best by more than tol for 20 epochs in a row; because tiny gains below tol do not count, the stop can come fewer than 20 epochs after the highest point. The final model keeps the weights from the best-scoring epoch.

Parameters:

  • result – Output of functions.tuning.nested_cv().

  • keys – (seed, fold) pairs to show (one column each).

Returns:

The figure (not shown or saved).

Entry point that tunes the MLP by nested CV and compares it with linear.

For each feature set, functions.tuning.nested_cv() tunes and scores the MLP on the outer folds, the linear baseline is cross-validated on the same seeds and folds, and the two are compared fold by fold. The test hold-out is never used:

python src/run_tuning.py                         # all seeds, sets A and B
python src/run_tuning.py --seeds 42 --feature-sets A   # quick timing check

Writes to results/:

  • tuning_outer_scores.csv: one row per (feature set, seed, outer fold): chosen setting, inner-CV best RMSE, outer RMSE/MAE/R², epochs run, max-iter hits and timings.

  • tuning_inner_grid.csv: mean and std inner-CV RMSE of all 35 settings for every (feature set, seed, outer fold).

  • tuning_selected_params.csv: how often each setting was chosen.

  • tuning_paired_vs_linear.csv: per-fold RMSE of MLP and linear and their difference (MLP minus linear).

  • tuning_summary.csv: headline numbers per feature set (see summary_row()).

  • tuning_warnings.txt: edge-of-grid and convergence warnings, if any.

Rounded tables and the figures (PNG + PDF) go to doc/generated/ for the HTML results page.

Error analysis¶

Entry point that finds the setups the models predict worst.

Each wind-tunnel setup (one chord, velocity and angle) gives one noise spectrum. This script computes the out-of-fold RMSE of every setup for the linear baseline and the tuned MLP, ranks setups by the MLP’s RMSE (the better model, so its failures are the interesting ones) and plots the worst spectra:

python src/run_error_analysis.py                     # sets A and B, 10 worst
python src/run_error_analysis.py --feature-sets B --n-worst 5

The MLP’s predictions are rebuilt from results/tuning_outer_scores.csv (run src/run_tuning.py first) by refitting each fold’s chosen setting; see functions.tuning.refit_outer_predictions(). This takes about 30 s per feature set. The test hold-out is never used.

Writes, for each feature set <fs>:

  • results/setup_rmse_<fs>.csv: every setup with both models’ RMSE and bias.

  • results/worst_setups_<fs>.csv: the worst setups by MLP RMSE.

  • doc/generated/worst_setups_<fs>.csv: a rounded copy for the docs.

  • doc/generated/worst_setups_spectra_<fs>.png and .pdf: their spectra.

Performance profiling¶

Runtime, memory, profiler and FLOP analysis of model training and prediction.

profile_model() fits a model once on all cross-validation rows (the test hold-out is dropped first, exactly as in functions.evaluate) and measures:

  • Time: median of repeated fit and predict calls, timed with time.perf_counter(). Repeats smooth out timer noise on fits that take only milliseconds.

  • Peak memory: with tracemalloc, which sees Python and NumPy allocations. Memory allocated directly inside compiled BLAS/LAPACK code is not seen, so the figure is a lower bound. Memory is measured in its own fit because tracemalloc slows code down and would distort the timings.

  • Profile: a cProfile run of one fit, listing where the time goes.

  • FLOPs: an analytical estimate (linear_flop_estimate()) for models that have one. Dividing it by the measured time gives the achieved FLOP rate, which shows whether a fit is limited by arithmetic or by Python and library overhead.

Example

>>> from functions.data_loader import load_airfoil_data
>>> from functions.physics_features import add_physics_features
>>> from functions.profiling import profile_model
>>> data = add_physics_features(load_airfoil_data())
>>> profile_model(data, "linear", "B").summary()
functions.profiling.N_TIMING_REPEATS = 20¶

Number of timed fit/predict repeats; the median is reported.

functions.profiling.N_PROFILE_LINES = 15¶

functions.profiling.linear_flop_estimate(n: int, p: int) → dict[str, float][source]¶

Estimate floating-point operations for the linear pipeline.

Counts for an n x p training matrix:

  • Input scaler: mean and variance (~3np) plus transform (~2np).

  • Target scaler: the same for one column (~5n).

  • LinearRegression: centring (~2np), then a least-squares solve with LAPACK gelsd (SVD based). For n >> p this costs about 2np^2 + 11p^3 FLOPs (R-SVD least squares, Golub & Van Loan, Matrix Computations). The 2np^2 term dominates.

  • Predict: input transform (2np), matrix-vector product (2np) and inverse target transform (2n).

These are leading-order counts for comparison with measured times, not exact operation counts.

Parameters:

  • n – Number of rows.

  • p – Number of input features.

Returns:

A dict with fit_flops and predict_flops.

functions.profiling.FLOP_ESTIMATES: dict[str, Callable[[int, int], dict[str, float]]] = {'linear': <function linear_flop_estimate>}¶

Model name -> FLOP estimate function (n, p) -> dict. Models without an entry are profiled without a FLOP estimate.

functions.profiling.profile_model(data: pandas.DataFrame, model_name: str, feature_set: str, n_repeats: int = 20) → ProfileResult[source]¶

Measure time, peak memory and the call profile of one model.

The model is trained on all cross-validation rows for the first seed in CV_SEEDS (the test hold-out is the same for every seed and is dropped). This is the largest training set used during model selection, so it gives an upper bound on per-fold costs.

Parameters:

  • data – Dataset with every column the feature set needs (see functions.evaluate.cross_validate()).

  • model_name – Key of functions.models.MODELS.

  • feature_set – Key of functions.feature_sets.FEATURE_SETS.

  • n_repeats – Number of timed fit and predict calls; the median is reported. Lower it for slow models.

Returns:

A ProfileResult.

Raises:

KeyError – If the model or feature set name is unknown.

Entry point that profiles runtime, memory and FLOPs of models.

Each requested model/feature-set pair is trained on all cross-validation rows (never the test hold-out) by functions.profiling.profile_model():

python src/run_profile.py
python src/run_profile.py --models linear --feature-sets B

Writes to results/:

  • profile_summary.csv: time, peak memory, estimated FLOPs and achieved FLOP rate per model/feature set.

  • profile_<model>_<feature set>.txt: the cProfile report of one fit.

A rounded copy of the summary is written to doc/generated/ for the HTML results page.

run_profile.write_doc_table(summary: pandas.DataFrame) → None[source]¶

Write the profile summary as a rounded table for the HTML documentation.

Times are converted to ms and memory to kB so the table reads at a glance on doc/results.rst.

Parameters:

summary – One row per model/feature set from functions.profiling.ProfileResult.summary().

Namespace with models and feature_sets lists.

Exploratory plots¶

Histogram of the target, scaled sound pressure level (SPL).

functions.plot_spl_distribution.plot_spl_distribution(df: pandas.DataFrame, bin_width_db: float = 1.0) → matplotlib.figure.Figure[source]¶

Plot the number of observations in each SPL bin.

Bin edges are whole multiples of bin_width_db so bars line up with round dB values. Dashed and dotted lines mark the mean and median, so any skew in the target is visible at a glance.

Parameters:

  • df – Dataset as returned by functions.data_loader.load_airfoil_data().

  • bin_width_db – Width of each histogram bin in dB. Must be positive.

Returns:

The created matplotlib figure (not yet shown).

Raises:

ValueError – If bin_width_db is not positive.

Overview scatter plot of SPL against every input feature.

functions.plot_spl_vs_features.plot_spl_vs_features(df: pandas.DataFrame) → matplotlib.figure.Figure[source]¶

Plot SPL against every input feature on a 2x3 grid.

Frequency spans several decades, so its axis is log-scaled. The unused sixth panel is hidden.

Parameters:

df – Dataset as returned by functions.data_loader.load_airfoil_data().

Returns:

The created matplotlib figure (not yet shown).

Scatter plots of SPL against each feature, split by chord length.

functions.plot_spl_by_chord_length.plot_spl_by_chord_length(df: pandas.DataFrame) → matplotlib.figure.Figure[source]¶

Plot SPL against each non-chord feature, one row per chord length.

Chord length takes only a handful of discrete values, so splitting by it reveals trends that are blurred in the pooled overview plot. The y-axis is shared so noise levels are comparable across rows.

Parameters:

df – Dataset as returned by functions.data_loader.load_airfoil_data().

Returns:

The created matplotlib figure (not yet shown).

Scatter plot of SPL against each physics-derived feature.

functions.plot_spl_vs_physics_features.plot_spl_vs_physics_features(df: pandas.DataFrame) → matplotlib.figure.Figure[source]¶

Plot SPL against log-frequency, Strouhal number and Reynolds number.

Strouhal and Reynolds numbers each span two to three decades, so their axes are log-scaled. Log-frequency is already logarithmic and is plotted on a linear axis.

Parameters:

df – Dataset with physics features, as returned by functions.physics_features.add_physics_features().

Returns:

The created matplotlib figure (not yet shown).

Entry point that displays the exploratory plots for the airfoil dataset.

The plotting functions live in their own modules (functions.plot_spl_distribution, functions.plot_spl_vs_features, functions.plot_spl_by_chord_length and functions.plot_spl_vs_physics_features); this script loads the data, adds the physics features, saves the figures used by the HTML docs to doc/generated/ and then shows every figure:

python src/explore_plots.py
python src/explore_plots.py --no-show   # only write the PNGs
explore_plots.DOC_FIGURES_DIR = WindowsPath('C:/Users/vasbr/OneDrive/Desktop/uni mech eng/2026s2/mma3001 numerical methods and machine learning/mma3001project/nummethodproject/doc/generated')¶

Directory for figures included by the Sphinx data page (doc/exploration.rst): <project root>/doc/generated.

explore_plots.save_explore_figures(df: pandas.DataFrame, out_dir: Path = WindowsPath('C:/Users/vasbr/OneDrive/Desktop/uni mech eng/2026s2/mma3001 numerical methods and machine learning/mma3001project/nummethodproject/doc/generated')) → list[Path][source]¶
